summary: A first-person narrative recalling the mythical creatures of the author's rural childhood, from the Banshee and Kelpie to the Wild Hunt. Each section pairs a creature's legend with a personal or family anecdote tied to a specific date or season. The author concludes that these tales bind people to their land and to each other, and remain emotionally real despite rational doubt.
one_line: A personal essay on countryside folklore creatures like the Banshee, Kelpie, Gryphon and Black Shuck, linked to family anecdotes from childhood.
key_facts: The author's grandmother recounted hearing the Banshee's sorrowful, piercing wail from a thicket near their home on a cold evening in November 2023; the Banshee is said to be an omen of death.
The Banshee is described as a spectral figure robed in grey with eyes aglow with foreknowledge of impending doom.
Around mid-September 2024, Old Man McCreedy claimed to have seen a magnificent horse by the lake, which he said was the Kelpie in a benevolent guise.
The Kelpie is a shapeshifting water spirit; anyone who mounts it while it is in the water is said to be dragged into the lake's depths.
Alice's grandfather said that as a boy in autumn 2025 he found a large nest on craggy outcrops above the village, which he believed was a Gryphon's aerie.
The Gryphon has a lion's body with an eagle's head and wings, and is seen in local tales as a guardian of treasures and protector of the realm.
In October 2026 the author and their brother saw Will-o'-the-Wisps on a forest path; parents said the lights were the spirits of the lost seeking their way home.
The Black Shuck is a ghostly dog with eyes like coals; farmers blamed it for lost livestock and odd footprints, and the author glimpsed a shadow in mid-September 2027 near the old stone walls.
The Green Man, with a face emerging from foliage in ivy and moss, is a benevolent symbol of rebirth; the author recalls standing beneath an old oak in spring 2028.
In late August 2029, spoiled milk, misplaced tools and strange footprints were blamed by the author's uncle on the Pookas, shape-shifters appearing as wild ponies or shadowy hares.
Midwife Mrs. Finnegan warned expectant mothers about Changelings, faerie doubles swapped for newborns who grow sickly and troublesome.
The Wild Hunt, a spectral cavalcade led by the Huntsman, was said to chase down lost souls; the author listened for it on a blustery night in December 2029.
